svg.font-family: Inter, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: Figure 2. Why the first hop deliberately does not rotate
svg.desc: A comparison of two designs for choosing the first relay. In the first design a fresh first relay is chosen for every circuit, which feels safer but means that over many sessions the probability of eventually choosing a hostile relay at least once approaches certainty, and one such occasion is enough for that relay to observe you. In the second design, the one Tor actually uses, the client keeps a small stable set of first relays for months, so the outcome is decided once: either the chosen relays are hostile, in which case you are exposed for the rotation period, or they are not, in which case you are safe for it. The design converts a slow accumulation of risk into a single decision. A band below gives the current parameters, which are two primary guards rotating on roughly a three and a half month schedule, and the history of the setting moving from three guards to one in 2014 and to two in 2022. A closing band explains what this means when a tunnel is placed in front of Tor.
svg.text: Figure 2: Why the First Hop Deliberately Does Not Rotate
Changing your entry point constantly feels safer. It is the opposite, and understanding why is the single most useful thing in this lesson.
a fresh first relay for every circuit, which Tor does not do

g.text: The appeal
No relay ever sees you twice. Nothing about you
accumulates anywhere. It sounds obviously correct.
What actually happens over time
Some fraction of relays are run by somebody who wants
to observe you. Each new circuit is a fresh draw from
that pool.
Draw enough times and the chance of picking a hostile
relay at least once goes to certainty. And once is enough,
because that relay then sees your real address.
So the risk is not spread. It accumulates.

svg.text: a small set of first relays, kept for months

g.text: The mechanism
Your client picks a small set of first relays and keeps
using them. Only the middle and exit change per circuit.
What that changes
The outcome is now decided once rather than sampled
repeatedly. Either your guards are hostile, and you are
exposed for the rotation period, or they are not, and
you are safe for the whole of it.
The trade, stated honestly
A small chance of sustained exposure, instead of a
near-certainty of brief exposure. Most people are
better off, and a few are worse off.

svg.text: The current settings, and the fact that they have changed three times
Today: clients use two primary guards, rotating on roughly a three and a half month schedule. The number is carried in the signed network consensus,
so it can be changed for the whole network without shipping new software.
The history matters: three guards originally, reduced to one in 2014 to narrow the points at which a client enters the network, and raised back to
two in 2022. A setting revised twice in a decade is one you should check rather than memorise.
What this means for putting a tunnel in front of Tor
Lesson 6.4 said the Tor Project does not recommend it, and this is the argument. A tunnel in front replaces a considered guard design with a single
permanent first hop that you chose, that sees every session you ever run, and that knows exactly who you are because you pay it every month.
That is a change to the threat model rather than a layer added on top of it. It may still be the right change. It is not a free one.
The general lesson: a defence that reduces each individual exposure can still increase your total exposure, if you sample often enough.
This is why "change your address constantly" is good advice in some places and actively harmful here. The right question is always what accumulates.
And note that this design is published, argued in public proposals, and revised when the argument changes. That is a property of the network, not a detail.
You can read the reasoning for the current value yourself, which you cannot do for any commercial provider's routing decisions.
